name: FOG battle threads

card.summary: Themed forum threads that put two faces side by side and ask members to vote on which one "fogs" (out-looks) the other, giving users a shared reference for what facial features read as strongest.
card.note: Opinion polls among forum members; thread votes are not a validated measure of attractiveness.

quick.overview:
A FOG battle is a recurring thread format on looksmax.org in which the original poster shows two people, usually women or fictional characters, and asks readers to pick which one "fogs" the other. Fogging is the forum's term for visually overpowering someone with a stronger face or frame.

The payoff for appearance-minded members is comparative: by arguing over why one face wins, users spell out the traits they consider decisive, such as bone structure, lower third, hair volume, height and frame, and use that vocabulary when judging their own look. The threads are informal polls; no research tests their rankings.
quick.how: Threads are usually themed: hair colour (blonde), region or phenotype labels (North Atlantid, Latina, Mediterranean), country matchups, a film or game cast, or mother versus daughter. The opening post may list each contender's strengths and weaknesses, or simply present two photos with a numbered choice, and replies vote and argue the case.
quick.risks: Threads rate real people's faces and bodies by label and often attract insulting banter, and members who post their own photos can receive harsh comments. Votes reflect the preferences of a self-selected forum audience.

lead: A FOG battle (also written "fog battle" or "fog off") is a themed comparison thread on looksmax.org in which two faces, or two groups of faces, are put side by side and members vote on which one "fogs" the other. "Fogging" belongs to the same family of slang as "mogging", which Wikipedia describes as asserting dominance over someone through appearance, a term that grew out of incel and manosphere communities and later reached TikTok [15].

For people working on how they look, the threads function as a shared vocabulary lesson. Each verdict has to be argued, so posters name the features that carry a face: frame size, height, phenotype, bone structure, lower third, hair volume and texture, and facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR) [1]. Members then borrow the same terms when judging which traits to work on in themselves. The format ran in many variants between at least 2021 and 2025, from region-versus-region "apex pheno" matchups to hair-colour, "full package" and pop-culture themes [7][8][9][11][12][14].

The threads are informal polls of a self-selected audience. Published attractiveness research looks at rater agreement, averageness, symmetry and cultural variation, and none of it has examined fog battles or tested their rankings [16][17].

angle.text: The threads give looksmaxxers concrete examples of which facial and body traits forum members rank highest. Participants use the feature-by-feature arguments as a reference when deciding what to improve in their own appearance.

paras: A typical opening post names a theme, shows photos of two contenders and asks readers to choose. The most compact version is a numbered pair of names with the instruction to pick the one that fogs. A more elaborate post labels each contender with a face type such as "True Eve Face", a regional phenotype, height and frame size, and then lists strengths and weaknesses [1]. In one such post, a contender is credited with frame, phenotype, lower third, bones and height, and marked down on dimorphism and FWHR, while her counterpart is credited with hair volume and texture [1].

The verb comes from the forum vocabulary around "mogging". Wikipedia notes that looksmaxxers may try to mog each other through looks, money or status, and links the word to the acronym AMOG, "alpha male of the group" [15]. In fog threads the contest is between two images rather than two forum members, and the question is which face or frame visually overpowers the other.

Some threads exaggerate the contrast between contenders. One 2022 thread titled as an "Albino vs Vantablack" matchup digresses into the origin of the intensifier prefix "tera", which a reply derives from the Greek word for "monster" and places above "giga" in the forum's scale of intensifiers [2].

Region and phenotype threads compare countries or ethnic groupings under labels such as "apex pheno": Colombia versus Lithuania, Portugal versus Belarus and Brazil versus Sweden all ran as separate threads in 2022 [7][8][9]. Latina and mestiza matchups ran in 2022 and 2023 [5][6], and an "Asians vs whites" thread appeared in 2021 [10].

Other threads fix a rule rather than a region. A 2021 "blonde fog battle" specified face only, so that frame and styling did not count [12], while a "full package" thread from the same year weighed more than the face [11]. A 2025 "classic" thread pitted two North Atlantid women against each other [4].

Lighter formats exist too: an Overwatch hero matchup between D.Va and Mercy applies the same vocabulary to fictional characters [14], and a "mom vs daughter" thread frames the comparison around inherited looks [13]. A 2025 thread asked forum members to be cast as their female equivalents under a "true Eve" label [3].

The format builds on rating culture from the forums that preceded looksmax.org. Wikipedia reports that the Perceived Sexual Levels (PSL) scale emerged in the 2010s on PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, rates facial attractiveness only, and that the terminology later spread to TikTok in the early 2020s [15]. Fog battles apply that comparative habit to pairs rather than to a single face on a numeric scale.

Among the threads that were loaded for this article, the earliest are from 2021 [10][11][12], with a cluster of country-based "apex pheno" threads in 2022 [7][8][9] and further matchups in 2023 to 2025 [3][4][5]. Because forum threads are hard to date reliably in aggregate, these years should be read as the dates of the specific threads, not as the origin of the term.

Press coverage of looksmaxxing has focused on the wider movement rather than on fog threads. Wikipedia lists Vice on "hunter eyes" in June 2023, Business Insider on looksmaxxing as a TikTok trend in November 2023, an analysis by Jamilla Rosdahl in The Conversation in January 2024, and BBC coverage in March 2024 [15]. None of these is documented as covering fog battles specifically.

Replies mix votes, feature lists and jokes. Posters cite height and frame (a wide frame is repeatedly treated as a strength), facial thirds and bones, hair, and ancestry-based labels such as North Atlantid or Mediterranean [1][4]. The dimensions that carry arguments in these posts overlap with what attractiveness researchers study: symmetry, averageness, youthful features, sexual dimorphism and clear skin are the features listed in encyclopedic summaries of that research [17][18].

Researchers who study ratings report that raters tend to agree about who is attractive, within and across cultures, according to an 11-part meta-analysis by Langlois and colleagues published in 2000 [16]. Encyclopedia summaries add that preferences also vary with culture, era, rater gender and context, and that several studies have been criticised for narrow samples or edited images [17][18]. Fog threads are not designed as research: voters are a self-selected audience and contenders are chosen by the poster.

Members describe the threads as a way to calibrate: seeing which contender wins and which listed features the voters credit gives a concrete picture of what the community treats as top tier [1]. Readers then map those traits to their own face and frame, for instance noting that hair volume or frame are listed as strengths, and choose which areas to work on, such as hair care, posture, or training for frame.
Because the contenders are mostly models, actresses or fictional characters, and the voting audience is a particular community, the reference points reflect that community's preferences [1][14].

Wikipedia reports that on some incel-linked forums users who are judged below average can be harassed, and that commentators link rating culture to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation [15]. Fog threads rate real people by label, and reply chains frequently include insulting banter aimed at contenders and at other posters. Members who post their own photos in comparison threads can draw harsh responses.

Critics cited by Wikipedia consider the PSL scale pseudoscientific, and the encyclopedia article describes looksmaxxing commentary as often linking the culture to harmful judgments about appearance [15]. Practitioners describe threads of this kind as entertainment and as a source of feature vocabulary.

No studies found. Related research on facial attractiveness, including a 2000 meta-analysis of rater agreement, studies features such as averageness and symmetry but has not examined fog battle threads [16][17].

timeline.event: Langlois and colleagues publish a meta-analysis finding that raters tend to agree on who is attractive.[16]
The PSL scale and associated rating vocabulary develop on PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net.[15]
Earliest fog battle threads in this record, including "blonde fog battle face only", "full package fog battle" and "asians vs whites".[10][11][12]
Series of country-versus-country "apex pheno" fog battles and Latina matchups run on looksmax.org.[6][7][8][9]
Themed variants include "mom vs daughter" and an Overwatch characters matchup.[13][14]
Vice covers "hunter eyes" (June) and Business Insider describes looksmaxxing as a TikTok trend (November); a Latina mestiza fog battle part 2 runs the same year.[5][15]
Rosdahl argues in The Conversation that TikTok algorithms draw young men toward looksmaxxing ideas; a fog battle of "unfoggables" between two models is posted.[1][15]
Fog threads continue, including a "classic" North Atlantid matchup and one casting forum users as female "true Eve" equivalents.[3][4]

lore.intro: Members treat fog battles as both entertainment and a way to calibrate what a top-tier face looks like [1]. Researchers have studied attractiveness ratings but not these threads [16].

claims.claim: Specific features, such as frame, bones, height and lower third, decide who "fogs"
claims.believers: Posters list strengths and weaknesses such as frame, phenotype, lower third, bones and height as the basis of a verdict [1].
claims.experts: No published research has tested these forum rankings; Wikipedia notes that parts of the related PSL scale are described as pseudoscientific [15].

claims.claim: Phenotype or country of origin predicts which face wins
claims.believers: "Apex pheno" threads pit countries against each other on the premise that regional looks can be compared head to head [7][8][9].
claims.experts: Encyclopedia summaries of attractiveness research report that preferences vary with culture, era and rater, and that several cross-group findings have been disputed [17][18].

claims.claim: The community vote reflects what people in general find attractive
claims.believers: Members present the thread outcome as a calibration of what a top-tier face looks like [1].
claims.experts: A 2000 meta-analysis found that raters tend to agree about who is attractive, though the studies used research samples, not self-selected forum voters [16].

claims.claim: Face-only and full-package rules change the outcome
claims.believers: Thread authors set "face only" or "full package" rules, implying that frame and styling shift who wins [11][12].
claims.experts: Encyclopedia summaries list posture, height, body proportions and movement alongside the face among rated features [18].

claims.claim: Contenders can be ranked on a single scale of "fogging" power
claims.believers: Intensifier prefixes such as tera and giga express degrees of dominance between contenders [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that critics consider the PSL scale pseudoscientific; no study has validated a fogging scale [15].

claims.claim: Comparison threads help members decide what to improve
claims.believers: Participants use the feature-by-feature arguments as a reference for their own looks [1][3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports commentators linking rating culture to body dysmorphia and harsh judgments of members [15].
